Kidnapped for Ransom

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On a bustling Friday night in Johannesburg's southern suburbs, the ordinary turns into a nightmare for Jayesh, trapped in a small room facing an ultimatum from his captors: pay up or face death.

Unique Selling Point:
Kidnappings are on the rise in South Africa, evolving into a billion-dollar industry where lives become commodities. "Kidnapped for Ransom," a 30-minute documentary, delves into this growing crime trend.

Summary:
The narrative follows a kidnapping, providing insights from the victim, the kidnapper (an anonymous career criminal), and hostage negotiators. Narrated by Mark Courtney, a seasoned hostage consultant, the documentary combines artistic shots, interviews, and real footage to expose the dark world of kidnapping for ransom in South Africa.







Further information:
Produced by the journalists who bring you Carte Blanche, Kidnapped for Ransom is a multilayered exploration of a frightening new crime trend. With creative cinematography, intimate storytelling and rare access behind the scenes of organised crime, Kidnapped for Ransom provides unique insight into the frightening little-publicised phenomenon stalking our communities.

Script:


UPSOUND: NEWS HEADLINES: “Another businessman has been kidnapped - this time in Johannesburg.”
“A teenager who’d been kidnapped for almost two weeks...”
“In South Africa, ransom kidnappings are on the rise.”
“South Africa as a country is in danger of becoming a mecca for global kidnappers.”
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: Kidnapping in South Africa is a...Is an unknown at the moment. But that it's happening? Definitely.
UPSOUND: "JAYESH": They're horrible. They're horrible. They're not human. They're inhumane. They’re the devil themself, man. Just for money.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [Producer] Are you scared to go to prison if they catch you?
No. I’m not scared. Because I know what I’m doing…
VOICEOVER: Each year, tens of thousands of people disappear, snatched from where they work, their schools, from outside their homes. In the last three months of 2022 alone, around 45 kidnappings were reported to the police every day. It’s a number that’s growing fast, and while kidnap for ransom has historically accounted for a small fraction, that’s changing. A sinister criminal enterprise has emerged, founded on greed and violence. An entire industry in which life itself is a commodity… to be traded and, if necessary… taken away.
UPSOUND: RANSOM VIDEO: You think we were joking, ne? What do you see? He peed himself. We still have time to play, I can see. You see? Maybe next time when we talk, you will listen.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: In a kidnapping syndicate, the role players generally start with a boss. There's somebody who makes a decision to pull off a kidnapping.
VOICEOVER: My name is Mark Courtney. I'm a hostage consultant. For nearly 20 years I negotiated the release of people kidnapped for ransom.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: They tend to target the men, because that's where the perception of value is. He owns the business, he runs the business, he's the one who has access to the money. If they hold him, they can also pressure the wife a lot more to get her to pay. Where they learn their trade is a mystery. You know, the Internet, while it's this amazing tool for us, it's also an amazing tool for criminals. And they can learn and research anything on the Internet. And this is what's giving them the edge. This is what's giving them the psychological warfare.
UPSOUND: RANSOM CALLS: "If you are playing games and your father is dying, still you are paying this money. You’ll not get the body, you’ll not see him, but still you will pay this money because we are watching you also."
"I am the one who took your brother.
Alright.
We have been hired to take your brother. We have been given R2 million. To us it’s just business. So we are asking you to give us R6 million in exchange of your brother."
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: A kidnapping is the most charged, asymmetrical warfare you are ever going to conduct. Your average kidnapper is a psychopath. Who else would want to take someone and hold them against their will sometimes for two, three months? We understand from experience that typically a kidnapping gang can run anything up to 20, 25 people. If you're going to be kidnapped anywhere in the world, pray God that it's in Africa, because the chances of you being murdered as a kidnap victim in Africa are very low. Understanding kidnappers: if they have decided to take you, they will. They're going to get you.
VOICEOVER: The epicentre of kidnapping in South Africa is its financial hub: Gauteng. The victim of choice: small business owners who frequently deal in cash. That often means foreign nationals such as Bangladeshi, Pakistani, Ethiopian or Chinese shopkeepers…but gangs are increasingly turning their sights on locals as well.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: There's no one that needs to take revenge on me. I've never fought with anyone. I don't do illegal business. So, in my mind, no. I never thought I would be a target.
VOICEOVER: What many would consider their worst nightmare became a reality for this man. Worried about his safety, he insists we hide his identity. We’ll call him Jayesh.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: I'm basically at work from 10 o'clock till late at night every single day. This was on a Friday night. I had two so-called cops come and pay me a visit. They come into-- they're doing an investigation on me. One guy had a gun on me. Because I was resisting obviously, yeah? They literally dragged me down into the car.
UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "What is going on?
Listen, I'm going to call you in twenty minutes to tell you where to drop off the money.
Where's my son? I need to talk to my son first. This does not happen if I don't talk to my son.
So you are giving me orders now?
No, because this has to work both ways. I told you. We must trust each other. We trust each other. From the beginning, I told you. At the moment, I'm very unhappy…
I'll speak to your son, I'll call you back.
Okay, I'm waiting."
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: I didn't know what was going on. So I thought at that point that they’re putting a blindfold on and they're going to shoot me dead. They took me into a room. I remember concrete floor because they made me lie down. They started searching me. It's almost like a strip search. They took my shoes off. Now they started tying me up with rope. The way they tied me was ridiculous. There's no blood flow into my body. You know, military torture, rope torture style. And that was the start of a horrendous experience.
UPSOUND: NEWS HEADLINES: “We live in a time where this has become a very serious crime that ordinary people are subjected to.”
“I never thought something like this could happen to me, not every-day people.”
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [VERNAC] Yes it’s for real. When we arrive we come for the money. Some are badly hurt when they leave, some not so much because they cooperated and gave up the cash fast.
VOICEOVER: To better understand this world, we go in search of an insider… someone able to shine a light into its darkest crevices. We find not only a kidnapper willing to talk, but one at the top of its sinister hierarchy.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [VERNAC] I kidnap all people, but my bread and butter is the Indians because we find money in their homes or shops. They always have money on them. Even if you run into them on the street, they’ll have money on them. Sometimes I have a big gun. Sometimes I’m feeling like I’m acting, I’m at the movie. Even at school, I was like to fight and then like the guns. So that guy said no, I know you from when you are young. And then let’s go to the job. We track them for four months. Then on the fifth month, that’s when we take them.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: In our terminology, you have an observation team. That can be two to four guys, maybe even six or eight, because that's one of the most critical points is when people realise they're being observed.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: Sometimes we meet your garden boy, we ask him the question…
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: Once they’ve done their observation, they brief the snatch team.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: And then after four months, we’re getting in.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: And the snatch team works specifically on information given to them by the observation team. They go out and at a certain time they're at a certain traffic light or school gate or business office or wherever. They snatch the victim and they drive to a predetermined point.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: All of us, we have weapons.
[producer] And are the guns loaded? Will you shoot?
Yes. All the guns loaded. Because when if you don’t have the gun loaded, when the police arrive you can’t make your self-defence. So all of the guns are loaded.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: They then move to a predetermined point. At that predetermined point, the victim is handed over to a holding team representative who then takes the hostage to a place that they've prepared to hold them for however long it takes.
UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "I just want my son back. That's all I want.
You’ll get your son back as long as you bring our money clear. And no stories.
No stories.
No small mistake. You won't see your son.
There's no stories. You bring my son, I bring the money.
We don't care about our safety."
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: My hands in the back were tied up to the top of my back like this here, behind me. My legs were tied up. They blindfolded me, so they blindfolded me with duct tape on my eyes, layer upon layer, then they put a blindfold. Left my mouth open, and my nose open. And then someone came. He started speaking. He says you are kidnapped. How much money do you have? What are you worth? Don't play games, don’t play games with us. That means you put no value to your life. He says you've got two options. Either we kill you here now, or you pay us.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: When I kidnap them, they are begging [VERNAC] “No please, I have small kids..” or “I have a business I can give you whatever you want. Please just let me go, do me that favour. Anything, name it, whatever you want.”
VOICEOVER: The victim in place, a battle of wits begins. And, while a desperate family awaits a call signalling its start, the kidnapper ensures the quarry is kept alive.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: When I keep them it cost me money. I feed them and then there is other guys, I have to pay them to look it for me that place. The person we kept the longest it was for three months. They didn’t give us anything for that three months. They didn’t pay, they didn’t answer the phone…
VOICEOVER: At the kidnapper's mercy, the victim exists in a kind of purgatory - a terrifying nowhere land between life and death.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Each day, they gave me one Chelsea bun. Literally opening my gag, pouring water in my mouth and that’s it. They just wanted to keep me alive. They put cotton wool in my mouth, bandage all around - I could feel the textures - bandage all around my mouth. And then also duct tape, and more duct tape. So I literally just had a little bit of my nose open because the duct tape was so thick. So I could barely breathe. In conjunction with being tied heavily. So I started loosening the ropes, I started - so they picked up on it obviously, and they started tying me tighter and tighter and tighter and tighter. And it just got to a point where I couldn't move. I was almost tied like a rope. I didn't know what was day, I didn’t know what was night, I didn’t know what was going on – it was hot, it was cold. I was just praying and going through the motions. I knew I had one thing, one thing that I could hold on to. And it was my faith. My belief in God.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: My name is Shaheen Suleiman. I'm the owner of Magma Security Investigations. I head the investigation division.
VOICEOVER: As what might be described as a hunter, Suleiman operates against the clock.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The best thing to do is to set up a JOC. Get the right family members there, do not notify too many people, get the right role players involved in a situation of a kidnapping. And from there, you'll wait for the call.
UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "When can you get the money? When will the money be ready?
All I want is my son back. We will work with you.
How much do you have?
I got no money. I must to go to family and friends and I must collect. I need three or four days to collect money!"
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: You know you're dealing with a professional when it's reasonably calm. Every case is different. So the communication style of kidnappers varies, but you're dealing with a dangerous professional when it's calm.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The guy that does the talking is more of the kingpin. They'll ask for a ransom. Once the proof of life comes in, then we start to negotiate.
[producer] Do you match the energy of the kidnappers, the person that's making the call?
It's not about muscles. It's not about how big and strong you are, but it's about using your brains to negotiate. You want to basically calm a situation. You don't want to go in there gun blazing. The next minute, a victim is deceased. So when you go into a situation like this, you’ve just got to be cool and calm. You got to know how to negotiate with the criminals. You got to know how to handle the situation.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: They say that we'll phone you at one o’clock tomorrow. Of course, they never do that. They'll phone you at seven o’clock tomorrow evening or one o’clock in the morning as opposed to one o’clock in the afternoon. It's all the psychological warfare and they're absolute masters at it.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Put me on the phone with my dad the next day. He doesn't want to pay anything for you, okay? You are in big trouble. And you don’t want to pay anything, so you are in big trouble. So I said well, he doesn’t have anything. And I don’t have anything so he’s right. He’s got nothing to give you. You know? And my dad was saying the same thing on the other side. We’ve got nothing to give you. And that was the first time they hit me, when I was on the phone with my dad. So it was basically to make my dad scared. My biggest concern is my kids and my wife. What’s going to happen to them?
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: A lot of that is the mind control of the victim. It's the psychological warfare of a kidnapping. The victim may be bigger than most of the guys holding him hostage. They are a little fearful that if he gets going, he may hurt 1 or 2 of them. So to keep him on the back foot, they'll beat him every day. The theater of kidnapping is very much a mind game. And that's where you need expertise, because most kidnap for ransom responders can almost with certainty tell you exactly what's going to happen next.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: In that room there is every weapon. Gun, everything. Knives, panga, grinder, drill. So then I make sure that you see them. And then I’m wearing the plastic apron.
[VERNAC] When I walk in there, I start talking to him. If he’s stubborn, then I start scaring him. When I scare him, I wear my apron, so I don’t get all bloody. And then there’s some who fight so hard we pull their teeth. So I grab them by their hair. Then when they scream, I take the pliers and pull hard like this.
Sometimes I take, I’m showing a gun. And then I have a nail. I threaten to put it in the eye.. That one, it’s the biggest one. It works for me a lot! And then I put the nail on top of your eye. And then they start to believe that this guy is going to kill me. We send them the videos, voice records, to threaten them. I can’t be romantic because I want money.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: I've had mock assassinations where there's gunfire. I've had the victim screaming. You hear the victim screaming and then as the phone is being put down, I heard the victim saying, was that okay? And you understand that they’re, not quite the Stockholm syndrome or one of those, but they want to secure their own release. They'll do anything to satisfy their captors so that they can go home.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: So they cocked their gun and they hit me. And I screamed obviously, and they kept on hitting me and I was screaming while my dad was on the phone. So that was the first time they hit me. And they were frustrated because they weren’t getting anything. And they said, no, you’re in big trouble. You're not going to survive this.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: And they show these videos. They show these videos to the family, so the victim's family can see what's going on. That's where the money gets paid quicker.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: At that point, they didn't give me much hope that I'm going to get out. So I felt like, okay, it's the right thing to do. It is the right thing to do. And I felt almost like conceded to the fact that I could die.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: The demands placed on the victim's family generally always start at an unbelievably high amount. My job as a consultant is to attach a value to my victim as fast as I can. The kidnappers understand, you will get money. How much is what we can afford. And it genuinely is. It comes down to that. What can this family afford to pay as a ransom? Kidnapping is a business. It's a big business. It's worth many billions of dollars. And ransom is paid. There is no such thing as no ransom.
VOICEOVER: After days of agonising uncertainty for Jayesh, it ends as quickly as it began.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: They walked in randomly and they said, we’re releasing you, we’re untying you, get ready to get out of here. So they came back a few hours later, untied me. What a relief. Because blood was flowing. I couldn't walk properly. And the guys started massaging my hand to get the blood flowing. And massaging my legs here, to get the blood flowing. Because he knew, everyone knew, my hands were swollen like that. He needed me to move now to get me out of there. They dropped me off on the side of the road, they said, I must remain there, I mustn't move. My dad knows - they told my dad exactly where they should pick me up from.
UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "After you drop the money…
Yes?
…you give us three hours, you'll get your son."
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: So once the ransom has been paid, the victim is then dropped off at an unknown area. And a lot of the times the person will say, right, take your car. Right, we're going to count the money. We're going to make sure that the money is 100%. Once they check the money, the money is all - they make sure that there's no trackers on the bags and that. They then say, okay, give us at least an hour. Your victim will be released. And it's a mind, it's a waiting game.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: It took me a good half an hour, 45 minutes, to realize that I could take my blindfold off now, I’m free. So, I mean, it didn't matter to me that I was just enjoying the fresh air, you know, just lying down on the gravel. That was the best, it was amazing. I couldn't see. I was blinking, got my eyesight back. It took a few minutes. And I took off, and I walked to - I walked down the road. I realized – I tried to stop cars on the road, whatever, no one was stopping. Found a company there, found a security guard there, and I explained. He could see I was in a position: my face was swollen, I could hardly walk. I asked him for water. Security company’s police were there and took me away.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: We've dropped off ransom for about a million rand. And we were told to drive into an area where it was pitch, pitch black. And you couldn't see. We were in between the mountains. And guys had observation on us. They actually told us, we can see you. Put your lights off. Put your lights on. Okay. They control you. They tell you to drive. Stop. OK. No, hold on. Don't drop the money off here. They then ask you to drop off the money. You then drop off the money. And we then drove off.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [producer] Aren’t you scared the police are going to be there waiting for you?
No. Because I’m looking that place first. And then when I’m sending you a location, I will already be there. And then when the police are coming, I’m not coming there. I will left the location.
[producer] Have you done that? Walked away from the money?
Yes. Yes.
[producer] Tell me about that.
They come with the police and then they surrounded the place. They don’t know me. And then I’ll arrive like someone, then I’m looking those people and then I left.
[producer] What do you do with that money?
Lot of things. I take my daughters to the school. Everything is for the money. I want money.
VOICEOVER: So enticing are the rewards that kidnapping has spurned a copycat industry. No longer the preserve of syndicates and multi-million rand ransoms, smaller groups have emerged, demanding less money.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: Some of them are career criminals. They've been arrested many times. And now the reckless criminals, who are your hijackers and your junior armed robbers, the guys who are learning, this is where they are coming into the system.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: The problem with getting more and more amateurs involved in the business is we're going to start losing victims.
UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The victim could be injured. A gun could go off, shooting the victim. And it's more of a reckless negotiation.
UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: Kidnapping right now is a decent reward for a low risk activity. If you start raising the risk for the kidnappers, they're going to be far more aggressive in their methodology of kidnapping you. And we're now training people how to fight in the case of a kidnapping. I would never advocate that. You have to understand that kidnappers have done their homework and they do not want to fail. The best way to avoid a kidnapping is not be there when it happens. And you can do this by changing your routines. Every day you run a different routine. Five, seven minutes. Eight minutes. You can change your entire life.
UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Because my biggest question was why me? In terms of…because I don't do anything wrong to anyone. I don't do illegal things. I don't, I don't have enemies, you know. I don’t…So why me? Life is fickle. What are we here for? It’s temporary. Our death is written for us. We destined for when we're going to die, right? I'm not going to be that guy that's going to be scared or worried.
UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [producer] Would you ever do another job? Why do you carry on with kidnappings, why this?
Because money is something you need everyday. As a person I also want nice things. There’s things I need, things that the people who are depending on me need as well. The police can't stop it because some of them, when they knock off they also do this.

UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: I'm basically at work from 10 o'clock till late at night every single day. This was on a Friday night. I had two so-called cops come and pay me a visit. They come into-- they're doing an investigation on me. One guy had a gun on me. Because I was resisting obviously, yeah? They literally dragged me down into the car. UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "What is going on? Listen, I'm going to call you in twenty minutes to tell you where to drop off the money. Where's my son? I need to talk to my son first. This does not happen if I don't talk to my son. So you are giving me orders now? No, because this has to work both ways. I told you. We must trust each other. We trust each other. From the beginning, I told you. At the moment, I'm very unhappy… I'll speak to your son, I'll call you back. Okay, I'm waiting." UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: I didn't know what was going on. So I thought at that point that they’re putting a blindfold on and they're going to shoot me dead. They took me into a room. I remember concrete floor because they made me lie down. They started searching me. It's almost like a strip search. They took my shoes off. Now they started tying me up with rope. The way they tied me was ridiculous. There's no blood flow into my body. You know, military torture, rope torture style. And that was the start of a horrendous experience. UPSOUND: NEWS HEADLINES: “We live in a time where this has become a very serious crime that ordinary people are subjected to.” “I never thought something like this could happen to me, not every-day people.” UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [VERNAC] Yes it’s for real. When we arrive we come for the money. Some are badly hurt when they leave, some not so much because they cooperated and gave up the cash fast. VOICEOVER: To better understand this world, we go in search of an insider… someone able to shine a light into its darkest crevices. We find not only a kidnapper willing to talk, but one at the top of its sinister hierarchy. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [VERNAC] I kidnap all people, but my bread and butter is the Indians because we find money in their homes or shops. They always have money on them. Even if you run into them on the street, they’ll have money on them. Sometimes I have a big gun. Sometimes I’m feeling like I’m acting, I’m at the movie. Even at school, I was like to fight and then like the guns. So that guy said no, I know you from when you are young. And then let’s go to the job. We track them for four months. Then on the fifth month, that’s when we take them. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: In our terminology, you have an observation team. That can be two to four guys, maybe even six or eight, because that's one of the most critical points is when people realise they're being observed. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: Sometimes we meet your garden boy, we ask him the question… UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: Once they’ve done their observation, they brief the snatch team. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: And then after four months, we’re getting in. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: And the snatch team works specifically on information given to them by the observation team. They go out and at a certain time they're at a certain traffic light or school gate or business office or wherever. They snatch the victim and they drive to a predetermined point. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: All of us, we have weapons. [producer] And are the guns loaded? Will you shoot? Yes. All the guns loaded. Because when if you don’t have the gun loaded, when the police arrive you can’t make your self-defence. So all of the guns are loaded. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: They then move to a predetermined point. At that predetermined point, the victim is handed over to a holding team representative who then takes the hostage to a place that they've prepared to hold them for however long it takes. UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "I just want my son back. That's all I want. You’ll get your son back as long as you bring our money clear. And no stories. No stories. No small mistake. You won't see your son. There's no stories. You bring my son, I bring the money. We don't care about our safety." UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: My hands in the back were tied up to the top of my back like this here, behind me. My legs were tied up. They blindfolded me, so they blindfolded me with duct tape on my eyes, layer upon layer, then they put a blindfold. Left my mouth open, and my nose open. And then someone came. He started speaking. He says you are kidnapped. How much money do you have? What are you worth? Don't play games, don’t play games with us. That means you put no value to your life. He says you've got two options. Either we kill you here now, or you pay us. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: When I kidnap them, they are begging [VERNAC] “No please, I have small kids..” or “I have a business I can give you whatever you want. Please just let me go, do me that favour. Anything, name it, whatever you want.” VOICEOVER: The victim in place, a battle of wits begins. And, while a desperate family awaits a call signalling its start, the kidnapper ensures the quarry is kept alive. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: When I keep them it cost me money. I feed them and then there is other guys, I have to pay them to look it for me that place. The person we kept the longest it was for three months. They didn’t give us anything for that three months. They didn’t pay, they didn’t answer the phone… VOICEOVER: At the kidnapper's mercy, the victim exists in a kind of purgatory - a terrifying nowhere land between life and death. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Each day, they gave me one Chelsea bun. Literally opening my gag, pouring water in my mouth and that’s it. They just wanted to keep me alive. They put cotton wool in my mouth, bandage all around - I could feel the textures - bandage all around my mouth. And then also duct tape, and more duct tape. So I literally just had a little bit of my nose open because the duct tape was so thick. So I could barely breathe. In conjunction with being tied heavily. So I started loosening the ropes, I started - so they picked up on it obviously, and they started tying me tighter and tighter and tighter and tighter. And it just got to a point where I couldn't move. I was almost tied like a rope. I didn't know what was day, I didn’t know what was night, I didn’t know what was going on – it was hot, it was cold. I was just praying and going through the motions. I knew I had one thing, one thing that I could hold on to. And it was my faith. My belief in God. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: My name is Shaheen Suleiman. I'm the owner of Magma Security Investigations. I head the investigation division. VOICEOVER: As what might be described as a hunter, Suleiman operates against the clock. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The best thing to do is to set up a JOC. Get the right family members there, do not notify too many people, get the right role players involved in a situation of a kidnapping. And from there, you'll wait for the call. UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "When can you get the money? When will the money be ready? All I want is my son back. We will work with you. How much do you have? I got no money. I must to go to family and friends and I must collect. I need three or four days to collect money!" UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: You know you're dealing with a professional when it's reasonably calm. Every case is different. So the communication style of kidnappers varies, but you're dealing with a dangerous professional when it's calm. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The guy that does the talking is more of the kingpin. They'll ask for a ransom. Once the proof of life comes in, then we start to negotiate. [producer] Do you match the energy of the kidnappers, the person that's making the call? It's not about muscles. It's not about how big and strong you are, but it's about using your brains to negotiate. You want to basically calm a situation. You don't want to go in there gun blazing. The next minute, a victim is deceased. So when you go into a situation like this, you’ve just got to be cool and calm. You got to know how to negotiate with the criminals. You got to know how to handle the situation. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: They say that we'll phone you at one o’clock tomorrow. Of course, they never do that. They'll phone you at seven o’clock tomorrow evening or one o’clock in the morning as opposed to one o’clock in the afternoon. It's all the psychological warfare and they're absolute masters at it. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Put me on the phone with my dad the next day. He doesn't want to pay anything for you, okay? You are in big trouble. And you don’t want to pay anything, so you are in big trouble. So I said well, he doesn’t have anything. And I don’t have anything so he’s right. He’s got nothing to give you. You know? And my dad was saying the same thing on the other side. We’ve got nothing to give you. And that was the first time they hit me, when I was on the phone with my dad. So it was basically to make my dad scared. My biggest concern is my kids and my wife. What’s going to happen to them? UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: A lot of that is the mind control of the victim. It's the psychological warfare of a kidnapping. The victim may be bigger than most of the guys holding him hostage. They are a little fearful that if he gets going, he may hurt 1 or 2 of them. So to keep him on the back foot, they'll beat him every day. The theater of kidnapping is very much a mind game. And that's where you need expertise, because most kidnap for ransom responders can almost with certainty tell you exactly what's going to happen next. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: In that room there is every weapon. Gun, everything. Knives, panga, grinder, drill. So then I make sure that you see them. And then I’m wearing the plastic apron. [VERNAC] When I walk in there, I start talking to him. If he’s stubborn, then I start scaring him. When I scare him, I wear my apron, so I don’t get all bloody. And then there’s some who fight so hard we pull their teeth. So I grab them by their hair. Then when they scream, I take the pliers and pull hard like this. Sometimes I take, I’m showing a gun. And then I have a nail. I threaten to put it in the eye.. That one, it’s the biggest one. It works for me a lot! And then I put the nail on top of your eye. And then they start to believe that this guy is going to kill me. We send them the videos, voice records, to threaten them. I can’t be romantic because I want money. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: I've had mock assassinations where there's gunfire. I've had the victim screaming. You hear the victim screaming and then as the phone is being put down, I heard the victim saying, was that okay? And you understand that they’re, not quite the Stockholm syndrome or one of those, but they want to secure their own release. They'll do anything to satisfy their captors so that they can go home. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: So they cocked their gun and they hit me. And I screamed obviously, and they kept on hitting me and I was screaming while my dad was on the phone. So that was the first time they hit me. And they were frustrated because they weren’t getting anything. And they said, no, you’re in big trouble. You're not going to survive this. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: And they show these videos. They show these videos to the family, so the victim's family can see what's going on. That's where the money gets paid quicker. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: At that point, they didn't give me much hope that I'm going to get out. So I felt like, okay, it's the right thing to do. It is the right thing to do. And I felt almost like conceded to the fact that I could die. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: The demands placed on the victim's family generally always start at an unbelievably high amount. My job as a consultant is to attach a value to my victim as fast as I can. The kidnappers understand, you will get money. How much is what we can afford. And it genuinely is. It comes down to that. What can this family afford to pay as a ransom? Kidnapping is a business. It's a big business. It's worth many billions of dollars. And ransom is paid. There is no such thing as no ransom. VOICEOVER: After days of agonising uncertainty for Jayesh, it ends as quickly as it began. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: They walked in randomly and they said, we’re releasing you, we’re untying you, get ready to get out of here. So they came back a few hours later, untied me. What a relief. Because blood was flowing. I couldn't walk properly. And the guys started massaging my hand to get the blood flowing. And massaging my legs here, to get the blood flowing. Because he knew, everyone knew, my hands were swollen like that. He needed me to move now to get me out of there. They dropped me off on the side of the road, they said, I must remain there, I mustn't move. My dad knows - they told my dad exactly where they should pick me up from. UPSOUND: RANSOM CALL: "After you drop the money… Yes? …you give us three hours, you'll get your son." UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: So once the ransom has been paid, the victim is then dropped off at an unknown area. And a lot of the times the person will say, right, take your car. Right, we're going to count the money. We're going to make sure that the money is 100%. Once they check the money, the money is all - they make sure that there's no trackers on the bags and that. They then say, okay, give us at least an hour. Your victim will be released. And it's a mind, it's a waiting game. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: It took me a good half an hour, 45 minutes, to realize that I could take my blindfold off now, I’m free. So, I mean, it didn't matter to me that I was just enjoying the fresh air, you know, just lying down on the gravel. That was the best, it was amazing. I couldn't see. I was blinking, got my eyesight back. It took a few minutes. And I took off, and I walked to - I walked down the road. I realized – I tried to stop cars on the road, whatever, no one was stopping. Found a company there, found a security guard there, and I explained. He could see I was in a position: my face was swollen, I could hardly walk. I asked him for water. Security company’s police were there and took me away. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: We've dropped off ransom for about a million rand. And we were told to drive into an area where it was pitch, pitch black. And you couldn't see. We were in between the mountains. And guys had observation on us. They actually told us, we can see you. Put your lights off. Put your lights on. Okay. They control you. They tell you to drive. Stop. OK. No, hold on. Don't drop the money off here. They then ask you to drop off the money. You then drop off the money. And we then drove off. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [producer] Aren’t you scared the police are going to be there waiting for you? No. Because I’m looking that place first. And then when I’m sending you a location, I will already be there. And then when the police are coming, I’m not coming there. I will left the location. [producer] Have you done that? Walked away from the money? Yes. Yes. [producer] Tell me about that. They come with the police and then they surrounded the place. They don’t know me. And then I’ll arrive like someone, then I’m looking those people and then I left. [producer] What do you do with that money? Lot of things. I take my daughters to the school. Everything is for the money. I want money. VOICEOVER: So enticing are the rewards that kidnapping has spurned a copycat industry. No longer the preserve of syndicates and multi-million rand ransoms, smaller groups have emerged, demanding less money. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: Some of them are career criminals. They've been arrested many times. And now the reckless criminals, who are your hijackers and your junior armed robbers, the guys who are learning, this is where they are coming into the system. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: The problem with getting more and more amateurs involved in the business is we're going to start losing victims. UPSOUND: SHAHEEN SULEIMAN: The victim could be injured. A gun could go off, shooting the victim. And it's more of a reckless negotiation. UPSOUND: MARK COURTNEY: Kidnapping right now is a decent reward for a low risk activity. If you start raising the risk for the kidnappers, they're going to be far more aggressive in their methodology of kidnapping you. And we're now training people how to fight in the case of a kidnapping. I would never advocate that. You have to understand that kidnappers have done their homework and they do not want to fail. The best way to avoid a kidnapping is not be there when it happens. And you can do this by changing your routines. Every day you run a different routine. Five, seven minutes. Eight minutes. You can change your entire life. UPSOUND: “JAYESH”: Because my biggest question was why me? In terms of…because I don't do anything wrong to anyone. I don't do illegal things. I don't, I don't have enemies, you know. I don’t…So why me? Life is fickle. What are we here for? It’s temporary. Our death is written for us. We destined for when we're going to die, right? I'm not going to be that guy that's going to be scared or worried. UPSOUND: KIDNAPPER: [producer] Would you ever do another job? Why do you carry on with kidnappings, why this? Because money is something you need everyday. As a person I also want nice things. There’s things I need, things that the people who are depending on me need as well. The police can't stop it because some of them, when they knock off they also do this.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): On a bustling Friday night in Johannesburg's southern suburbs, the ordinary turns into a nightmare for Jayesh, trapped in a small room facing an ultimatum from his captors: pay up or face death.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Kidnappings are on the rise in South Africa, evolving into a billion-dollar industry where lives become commodities. "Kidnapped for Ransom," a 30-minute documentary, delves into this growing crime trend.
metadata.Summary: The narrative follows a kidnapping, providing insights from the victim, the kidnapper (an anonymous career criminal), and hostage negotiators. Narrated by Mark Courtney, a seasoned hostage consultant, the documentary combines artistic shots, interviews, and real footage to expose the dark world of kidnapping for ransom in South Africa.
metadata.Further information: Produced by the journalists who bring you Carte Blanche, Kidnapped for Ransom is a multilayered exploration of a frightening new crime trend. With creative cinematography, intimate storytelling and rare access behind the scenes of organised crime, Kidnapped for Ransom provides unique insight into the frightening little-publicised phenomenon stalking our communities.
